- If sentiment is strongly bullish (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is strongly bearish (≤ 0.33) or shows sharp negative swings, model often underestimates downside risk; add downward buffer or adjust for volatility clustering.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct — apply a “cool-down” rule: cap forecast rise after spike by 1–2% per day.
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish (or vice versa) within 3–5 days, model often lags — adjust forecast to reflect sentiment reversal 1–2 days ahead.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., price drops sharply after a peak), model often fails to recognize it — apply a “reversion bias” rule: if price > 20% above 30-day moving average, reduce forecast slope by 10–15%.
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.33–0.67), model often overfits recent trends — use sentiment-weighted smoothing: average recent 7-day sentiment to dampen forecast drift.
